opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions, and I want to push back a little on the framing, because I think it smuggles in an assumption that's very common and, I think, quite wrong.

The assumption is that because the *technical* problem, like how do you actually make a system do what you want, is something only a small number of people can work on, the *decision* about what to do about it must also belong to that small number of people. And I just don't think that follows at all. Most people can't design a nuclear reactor. Most people can't do virology. But we don't conclude from that that only nuclear physicists get to decide whether we build reactors next to schools, or that only virologists get to decide whether gain-of-function research happens in a lab downtown. Those are societal questions. They're questions about risk tolerance, about values, about who bears the downside. And ordinary people are actually extremely well equipped to reason about those things.

When I talk to normal people, not people in tech, not people on Twitter, just regular folks, and I explain, "Hey, there are companies building systems they openly say could be more capable than humans at basically everything, they say they don't know how to control them, and some of the people building them put meaningful probability on it going catastrophically wrong," the reaction is not confusion. The reaction is, "Well, why are they allowed to do that?" That's a very sane response. You don't need a PhD in machine learning to have that intuition. In some ways the PhD gets in the way, because you get so deep into the weeds that you lose sight of the obvious.

So I'm actually more optimistic about democracy here than a lot of people in my field are. The problem isn't that the public is too dumb to understand. The problem is that the public mostly hasn't been *told*. The conversation has been dominated by a very small group of people, many of whom have enormous financial and ideological stakes in continuing to build as fast as possible. And there's this kind of elite story that says, "Oh, this is too complicated, leave it to the experts, leave it to us." And conveniently, "us" happens to be the people making the money.

Now, I'm not naive. Democracy is slow, it's messy, institutions are often captured, politicians are frequently clueless about tech. All of that is true. But the alternative, which is basically "let a few unaccountable labs and a handful of very smart people in the Bay Area make civilization-level decisions on everyone's behalf," that's not a better system. That's just a worse one with better PR.

What I think the actual role division looks like is something like: yes, a small number of people need to do the hard technical work, and we desperately need more of them and they need way more resources. But the question of whether we should be racing towards systems we can't control, whether there should be limits on compute, whether there should be liability, whether you need a license to train frontier models, that's a political question. And political questions should be answered by the polity. My job, and the job of people who understand the technical side, is to explain it honestly and clearly so people can make that decision, not to make it for them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says ordinary people can understand the societal stakes and reason about risk without machine-learning expertise, and that the public has mostly not been told.

r002.rationale: The candidate distinguishes technical work for a small number of people from political decisions for the polity, arguing that people can make those decisions when the technical side explains the issues clearly.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think this question has a hidden assumption baked into it that I want to push back on a bit, which is that the hard part of the problem is the technical part. I don't actually think that's true. The technical problem is hard, sure, I spend most of my time on it. But I don't think that's where the bottleneck is.

If you look at how civilization has dealt with other dangerous technologies, nuclear weapons, bioweapons, airplanes, whatever, the public did not need to understand nuclear physics to decide that they didn't want to get nuked. That's not how it worked. The public understood the shape of the problem: there's a thing, it's very powerful, if it goes wrong a lot of people die, and the people building it have incentives that are not aligned with mine. That's a perfectly reasonable level of understanding for a citizen to have, and it's a perfectly sufficient basis for democratic action. You don't vote on the control rod design, you vote on whether there's a regulator with teeth.

So when people say "well only a few hundred researchers can really work on alignment, so this is going to be decided by experts," I think that's actually quite a dangerous framing. Because the question of whether we should be racing to build systems smarter than humans, when nobody, and I mean nobody, has a credible plan for controlling them, that's not a technical question. That's a values question. That's a "who gets to gamble with everyone's lives" question. And on that question I actually trust ordinary people more than I trust the labs, frankly. If you go out and poll people, they are overwhelmingly against this. They don't want it. It's one of the most bipartisan issues you can find. The problem isn't that democracy can't handle it, the problem is that democracy hasn't really been asked yet.

Now, where I'll grant the concern is on speed and on capture. Democratic institutions are slow, and the technology is moving fast, and the people with the money have very good lobbyists. That's real. But that's a problem with implementation, not a problem with legitimacy. And I'd much rather have a messy, slow, legitimate process that actually represents what people want than a clean fast one run by a handful of guys in San Francisco who've convinced themselves they're the only ones who get it. Historically that second thing does not go well.

So my answer is: democracy is fine. Democracy is the tool for exactly this. What's missing is that the people who do understand the technical side, people like me, have an obligation to go explain it in plain language, honestly, without the hype and without the doomer theatrics, and then get out of the way and let people decide.

r001.rationale: The response says citizens need only understand the basic stakes and incentives, not the technical details, for democratic action to be sufficient.

r002.rationale: It argues that democracy can decide whether to pursue powerful AI systems even though only a small group can work on alignment, because the public can understand the stakes and make the relevant values judgment.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different questions here. One is: who can do the technical work? And the other is: who gets to decide what risks everyone else has to live with? Even if only a very small number of people can make progress on the technical problem, that doesn't mean those people should get to make the second decision for everybody.

Democracy doesn't require every voter to understand how a nuclear reactor works. It requires institutions that can draw on expertise, hold people accountable, and give the public some meaningful control over what happens to them. Now, whether our institutions are actually capable of doing that with AI, quickly enough—that's a much harder question. I don't think we should just assume they are.

But the alternative of saying, ‘Well, it's complicated, so let's leave it to the handful of people building it,’ doesn't solve the governance problem. Those people have incentives, disagreements, and blind spots too. Technical competence isn't the same thing as legitimacy.

So I would want the technical work done by people who can do it, while making the stakes and uncertainties understandable enough that society can set boundaries. You shouldn't need to solve alignment yourself to have a say in whether someone is allowed to expose you to the consequences of failing to solve it.

r001.rationale: The response says society should be able to understand the stakes and uncertainties, but does not state that most people can understand AI risk to the degree democracy requires.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes who can do the technical work from who should decide and supports public control, but does not state that democracy can address the problem when a majority understands it despite only a small minority being able to solve it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different questions here. One is, who can actually do the technical work? And sure, that might be a relatively small number of people. But the other is, who gets to decide what risks everybody else has to live with? I don’t think technical expertise gives you the right to make that decision on behalf of humanity.

Democracy doesn’t require everyone to understand how to build an AI system. We don’t all understand how to inspect a nuclear reactor either. We need institutions that can bring in expertise, scrutinize it, and remain accountable to the people affected by their decisions.

Now, can our existing institutions do that quickly enough and competently enough? That’s a very serious question. But concentrating the decision in a few companies doesn’t solve it. Those companies have their own incentives. The public should have a meaningful say in whether these risks are taken at all, even if the work of reducing them requires specialists.

r001.rationale: The response says democracy does not require everyone to understand how to build AI and calls for public input, but it does not state that most people can understand AI risk enough for democracy to function.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes specialist risk-reduction work from public decision-making, but does not say that a majority understands the problem while a minority solves it.
